summary: Hexagonal wooden light on Harbour Point, Gabarus Bay, lit in 1890; a community society had it moved 40 feet back from an eroding cliff in 2015.

access.note: Grounds open year round; the tower is not open to the public.

events.note: Built by Neil McNiell under contract for $650; total construction expenditure $748.33 (1890 Department of Marine notice, as printed by Lighthouse Friends).
Seventh-order dioptric lens in use 1922 to 1941.
End of the seventh-order dioptric lens period (NSLPS).
Lighthouse Friends says a light and foghorn were placed on Rouse Point; the Coast Guard list places the Gabarus light on Harbour Point.
Slid about 40 feet back from the eroding cliff on 26 and 27 November 2015 (Lighthouse Friends gives 26-27 November; SaltWire says Thursday into Friday), by T&J Demeyere Properties.
Restored to its original design, with new windows, framing and paint.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1891 comes from Rowlett's Lighthouse Directory as echoed by a tourism guide, which also says the light was first established in 1890. The Department of Marine's 1890 notice (as printed by Lighthouse Friends) says the tower was put in operation on 1 November 1890, and the Register gives circa 1890. The story uses 1890.

A tourism guide says the tower standing today was built 1955 to 1962 as a replacement for the original. The Register, Lighthouse Friends and the 2015 news all describe the 1890 wooden tower, moved in 2015, so the story treats the 1890 tower as the one standing today.

SaltWire and Lighthouse Friends give 40 feet; the Regeneration Works case study gives 15 metres. The story gives both, and treats 40 feet as the better-supported figure because two independent accounts agree on it.

corrections.why: The 1890 Department of Marine notice, as printed by Lighthouse Friends, gives 1 November 1890 as the date the tower went into operation; the Register dates it circa 1890. The 1891 date traces to a tourism guide.

notes_for_editor: Sources: the Register and the Coast Guard list are authoritative for the tower and the light; Lighthouse Friends (copyright, used for facts and short quotes only) carries the 1890 notice, the keeper dates and the 2015 to 2017 history, and is secondhand for the 1890 notice. Keeper names: only Hardy is matched to a primary source (the 1904 keeper table, matched by position on the same OCR line, scan p. 230; the printed page is not confirmed). J. McDonald and Morrison rest on Lighthouse Friends alone. The 1912 Department statement names Gabarus in the Cape Breton list, but its keeper column was not matched by position, so it is not used. Unresolved: whether the light shows from Harbour Point or from Rouse Point (Lighthouse Friends says a light and foghorn went on Rouse Point in 1982; the Coast Guard list gives Harbour Point with range 8 nm); the 1955 to 1962 replacement claim in the tourism guide and NSLPS; the 15 metre move distance; the Canadian newspapers (no free Canadian newspaper archive; the Chronicling America search returned nothing usable). The CBC report on the move could not be read (timeout). No storm, wreck or rescue tied to the station turned up in the Marine reports or the sources read, so the story has no storms chapter. The 2017 transfer outcome after the society declined is not in the sources read. Research budget: about 7 page reads and 1 newspaper search; no full keeper roster from a primary source for 1931 to 1950. Chapter count: the story has four chapters plus Today (five headings), each with sourced material; the editor may trim if the shape rule is strict. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1904 keeper table entry for Hardy was read from the page image (scan p. 230, printed p. 217): "Hardy, John | Gabarus | Nov. 22, 1890 | 200 00". NSLPS gives the light as both operational (light details) and not still operating (summary table); the story states that. The 1955 to 1962 span is attributed to the tourism guide and NSLPS. The 2015 move is dated 26 and 27 November (Lighthouse Friends) with SaltWire placing it on Thursday and Friday. The contest is a public-vote campaign, not crowdfunding; the Regeneration Works case study calls it crowdfunding, which the story does not use.
